**The masts on her breadth.** Forfait's Table VII gives the lugger's masts as multiples of
her breadth and her yards of her length; on her length the masts would have given three
quarters of the canvas his own rule of 4.037 L B asks, and on her breadth they give five per
cent over it. Taken on the breadth, as the table's own column says; for the lead, since the
centre of effort then falls a little before the middle where Forfait has it abaft (0.016 L
before against 0.024 L abaft): the yards' slings a third along them and the tacks at the
masts' feet put it there, and the hull's lateral centre was moved abaft to balance her
(above) rather than the canvas moved.

**What she sails** (the hierarchy truths of M5 §19 extended to six vessels,
`tests/test_ships_hierarchy.py`; fifteen knots of true wind, plain sail, all hands called
first for the two new hulls, since the smack's eight men in one watch could not set her
canvas in the sweep's time):

| True wind angle | 50° | 60° | 70° | 90° | 110° | 130° | 150° | 170° |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| The lugger, knots | 5.4 | 6.6 | 7.3 | 8.25 | 8.2 | 7.7 | 6.6 | 6.2 |
| The smack, knots | 4.0 | 5.4 | 5.8 | 6.2 | | 5.5 | | |

The lugger's best course to windward 52° and her nearest 44° (the cutter's 58° and 48°, the
schooner's 58°), heeling 11.3° with the wind abeam; the smack's best 58° and nearest 46°, as
the cutter. Their far-detail polars (`ships.far_polar`) come to within a tenth of these (the
lugger's row at fifteen knots peaks at 8.27, the smack's at 6.0).

**The lug and its dip.** The lug's curve and its trim were already in the sails' tables;
the dipping lug (`SailSpec.dipping`) is new. Against its mast (on the weather side) a lug
draws two thirds of its area (`LUG_AGAINST_MAST_AREA`, judgement: Forfait p. 6 and Lescallier
p. 392 say only that it sets badly so). The tack lowers the two dipping lugs at `ready about`
("lower the foresail and the mainsail") and dips them as she comes through the wind, a minute
and a half (`dip_s`, judgement), finishing only when they are hoisted on the new lee side:
the lugger's tack in fifteen knots takes 136 seconds. A missed stays hoists them again
(`hoist_lugs_s`, 45) before the evolution fails. The wear dips them as the wind comes aft.
`dip the foresail` alone: lower 30 s, shift 60, hoist 60. Hove to under the fore lug she
forereached at 4.7 knots; the heave-to lowers both dipping lugs, and she lies 65° off at 2.2
knots under the mizen and the jib. Left for milestone 7, said in the spec: the gybe of a lug,
the dip in a boxhaul and in filling away, and the strain of a lug aback against its mast
(Forfait's rule 2).

### The world's business (item 2; `freesail/world/business.py`, `data/business.yaml`)

Every figure of `data/business.yaml` is judgement and says so: the population at density 1
(three traders in port, three at the edges, four fishermen, a cruiser a side), the hourly
chances (a trader 0.25, a fisherman 0.08), `most_ships` 16, the least ratio of prices 1.3,
the cargo 30 to 120 tons, the wait in port already done 1 to 11 hours, the fishing grounds
10 to 80 fathoms two miles off the coast with a home within 45 miles, the trips 8 to 30
hours, the third of the in-port traders outward bound, the rumours within 250 miles.

**What the guard refused, and the mends.** The first draw put the in-port traders at the
outer road with plans laid as if at sea, and the far-detail guard refused a third of them
(Cawsand Bay to the Sound across Penlee, Bertheaume to St Mary's); arrivals at the northern
edge, on the Bristol Channel's side, were refused for Brest and St Mary's across Cornwall.
Now a ship drawn in port lies at the anchorage and is planned out by her port's own track
(`departing`, the vessel spec's new key, as `_in_port` plans one that sails); an arrival is
drawn only at an edge point whose straight line to the port's approach is clear; a route
refused once is not drawn again that day; and a port whose own tracks the guard refuses is
left out: **Roscoff** (its track to sea from the road of the Isle of Bas crosses the island
on the guard's straight line, at 48° 47.7' N 4° 00.1' W) and **St Mary's** (no tracks; the
straight line from the mouth of St Mary's Sound to the road crosses the Garrison). Both are
the tracks' data, for the lead; a far ship sailing those lines would go through the land.
The first draw of seed 7 tried thirty-four plans for eleven ships, a second and a half
of the planner's sea routes each under the profiler; now one plan a ship, the draw at the
start in seven seconds on the loaded machine.

**The draw at seed 7, a day and a half in the Channel** (`merchant-cutter.yaml` with
`business: on`, the region channel-west, the start 05:00 on 12 June 1805, run 36 hours of
ship's time in 685 seconds at a load of four to six; `scratchpad/p43b/business_day.py`):

| | Drawn | Where | What | How it ended by 36 hours |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| At the start: 3 traders in port | the Danish brig *Haabet*, Brest to Falmouth, 81 tons of wine; the Danish brig *Fortuna*, Falmouth outward bound for 47° 55' N 5° 24' W, 88 tons of coal; the American schooner *Sally*, Plymouth to Brest, 96 tons of pilchards | the Bay of Brest, Carrick Road, Plymouth Sound | neutral flags for the enemy's port (Britain and France at war) | *Haabet* ran for shelter three times in the thick and lies in Bertheaume road, in port; *Fortuna* still off Falmouth (50° 01' N), her passage taken up afresh seven times by the crewed promotion's fold-backs within the player's range and twice run for shelter; *Sally* off the Iroise |
| 3 traders at the edges | the Danish brig *Christiane* for Brest (pilchards), the American schooner *Enterprise* for Brest (coal), the Portuguese brig *Esperança* for Falmouth (brandy) | the western and southern edges | | *Enterprise* in at Brest at 112080 (31 hours) and gone; the others nearing their ports |
| 4 fishermen | the smack *Endeavour* on the Poll Bank from St Mary's (10 hours); the luggers *Saint-Yves* in the Iroise (15 hours) and *Jeune-Henriette* on the soundings south-west of Ushant (20 hours) from Brest; the smack *Industry* on the oozy ground off the Eddystone from Plymouth (9 hours) | on their grounds | | *Endeavour* home and gone at 13 hours, *Industry* at 15, *Saint-Yves* at 29½ (her trip, then the thick); *Jeune-Henriette* twice evading a stranger, her twenty hours worked, bound home |
| 2 cruisers | the British cutter *Sparrowhawk* off the Lizard, the French brig-sloop *Diligente* off the Sept Iles | on their stations | | keeping station; *Sparrowhawk* investigated a stranger three times and went back to her station each time (before the friend's mend below, a cruiser took the same neutral for a stranger every minute) |
| 8 by the hourly draw | 5 traders (Plymouth's four, one outward bound; one from Brest outward bound), 3 fishermen (two from Brest, one from Plymouth) | in port | coal, copper ore, pilchards, salt beef, wine | at sea, or in port again after a run for shelter |

Twenty ships in all, sixteen at sea at the end; the player's lookout at anchor in Carrick
Road hailed twelve sails in the day and a half. No ship left at the edge within the 36
hours: the outward-bound traders that got clear of the land were still on their way to
their marks beyond it (the edge's leaving is proved by `tests/test_business.py`). The run shows two
things of package 43's brains, not this package's: a ship drawn at Brest's anchorage in the
Bay of Brest starts "at anchor" and not "in port", since the port's reach is read from the
outer road (Bertheaume) eight miles off, so her drawn wait is not counted; and the thick
weather of the climatology sends every ship near the land into a road by turns, where she
waits her twelve hours in port again (*Haabet*, *Friendship*).

**The rumours.** Off where the business is off: the recorded passages' boats bring what they
brought. Drawn at the start of the same day for the three ports with markets the boat
goes to: at Falmouth "The talk on the quay, as the boat's crew heard it: wine cheap at
Brest, coal dear at Brest and salt cheap at Brest. Rumour, no more."; at Plymouth copper
ore, pilchards and coal dear at Brest; at Brest pilchards cheap at Plymouth, copper ore cheap
at Falmouth and wine dear at Plymouth (the war's half on the enemy's goods in the tables;
`tests/test_business.py` checks every word true by them).

### The ports' faults (item 3)

**(a) The let-go** (`scripts.too_little_water`, `ComeToAnchorScript`). The trade trial's
schooner let go at 19:23 in four fathoms and a half, the master's tide leaving two at low
water for her eleven feet, and lay aground on the ebb at 21:48. The cast at the let-go, less
the master's own fall to low water, must leave her a fathom under her keel; if not, the
anchor is belayed and she stands back once for the water where the lead called the ground
good at the decision, a minute at least (`STAND_BACK_LEAST_S`) and ten at most, and rounds
to there. From the trial's old trajectory (a checkpoint at 52000, before the beating rule's
mend): "Belay the anchor: the lead gives four fathoms and a half; by the master's tide two
fathoms at low water, and she draws 11 feet. Sheet home again; stand back for ..." at 19:23,
"The lead calls five fathoms" at 19:28 and the bower let go in five at 19:28:50; afloat
through the ebb. `tests/test_anchor.py` carries her onto that shoal from six fathoms and a
half and proves it. With the beating rule's mend (below) the trial itself now comes in at
19:41 into fifteen and a half and never wants the cast: the xfail lifted, the trial
re-pinned (the table below).

**(b) The Goulet on the flood** (`Ports._turn_high`). From the owner's wardroom save, loaded
by the game's replay to the tick and the pilot given the conn (`scratchpad/p43b/
goulet_probe2.py`, run with `-I`; `tests/test_ports.py` the slow test):

| From | Before (the head) | After |
|---|---|---|
| 113000 (12:23) | aground on the Mingan at 13:03 | the berth at 13:44, at anchor 13:50 in 13 fathoms; the least water 11.6 fathoms |
| 114000 (12:40) | aground on the Mingan at 13:05 | the berth at 13:46, at anchor 13:56 in 14 fathoms; the least water 12.3 fathoms |
| 114700 (12:52) | the berth at 13:50 (package 45c's case) | the berth at 13:50; the least water 10.9 fathoms |

The wind north-westerly, 308° to 320°, at ten knots; the flood setting her up the Goulet and
onto the rocks as she turned in from the line of Bertheaume. His aim is held up to the side
the stream sets from by the set over the leg as she will lie (`_made_good_on`: her heading as
near as she lies with a point of margin for the wind's drawing ahead, which the first
version lacked: the wind drew from 308° to 320° and his aim came out none), capped at three
cables, in clear water and with a clear line, recomputed at each look until it holds.

**(c) Torbay** (`data/tides/streams.yaml`, the area `torbay`, between Hope's Nose and the
Berry Head): the bay was the open Channel's water.

| At Brixham road (the anchorage) and in the bay | Springs, the strongest in a day | Neaps |
|---|---|---|
| Before (mid-channel) | 1.35 knots | 1.11 knots |
| After (torbay: 0.2 and 0.1 by the table) | 0.17 knots | 0.14 knots |

Off the Berry Head the Channel's stream runs as before. The rates are judgement (Imray 1874:
"there is little stream in the bay"; the modern atlas's under a quarter of a knot from memory,
unverified); the directions' book gives the bay none.

**(d) The pilot's words.** His corrections of under two points (`PILOT_TRIM_POINTS`) are
routine lines; his turns of two points and more, "trim to it" (now routine too) and his
warnings stand. The intent scenario's conn from Bertheaume had added two hundred and forty
notable lines to its log (45c's open item 3).

### The beating flap (item 4; `captains.Judgement._course_verdict`)

The trade trial's captain traded `on passage` and `beating` every two minutes at 08:58 as the
evasion ended (17880 to 18240): the beating rule and the passage rule were two rules, each
state's first course, shaped on the edge of the wind, giving the other's verdict. One rule
decides now: the course last shaped against the wind of the minute, not laid nearer than her
close-hauled angle and the shaping's half point (`COURSE_NOT_LAID_MARGIN_POINTS`), laid only
half a point freer (`beating_band_points`, the doctrines'), and between the two as it was; and
the state moves on a verdict that has stood `beating_dwell_minutes` (ten, as `gale_over_minutes`).
Both thresholds are in the merchant's, the King's ship's, the cruiser's, the packet's, the
commodore's and the fisherman's doctrines. In the trial the flap is gone; she beats from
31740 to 38340 and from 44880 to 56340.

**Found on the way**: the cruiser's `friend made out` left her free to take the same sail for
a stranger the next minute (the business's *Bayonnaise* off the Isle of Bas investigated a
neutral lying in Roscoff every minute for a day); a friend made out is now remembered as one
given up (`Judgement._transitions`). No pin moved for it (the four below are the
dwell's).

### The regatta's two findings, at the merge (the lead's word of 2026-10-17)

Package 44 merged on the head (`62f0981`) and into this branch (`a93d1c6`); its two small
findings in the captain and the course are mended here (`47014f7`):

- **A mark passed abeam far off** (`reckoning.WAY_PASSED_WITHIN_NM`, two miles): the
  master's way by marks and the captain's legs (`Captain._passed`) take a mark as passed
  abeam only within two miles of it or of the line to it (`geo.off_the_line_m`, the
  cross-track distance), where the bearing alone abaft the line's beam had passed a water
  mark far to windward. `tests/test_via.py` has it both ways.
- **Under way with no sail set** (`Captain._sail_if_none`): entering on passage, beating or
  running for shelter under way with none set, he makes plain sail (the topsails alone over

## Package 42b: the consent brief revised for 6c (2026-10-17)

Package 42b (decision 48; spec M6 §15 as built; the brief in `docs/dev/M6-WorkPackages.md`).
It ran in two steps. First the revision was drafted for the owner
(`docs/playtests/drafts/consent-brief-6c-draft.md`: the whole file marked, fifteen
numbered changes, each with the sentence as it stood, the sentence proposed and a reason,
four of them beyond the package's brief). Second, after the owner's rulings of the same
day (all fifteen approved as drafted, and the session-kind fix with the race named among
the kinds of session), the approved sentences were written into
`docs/agents/ConsentBrief.md` to the character, by a script that asserts each
replacement; a check confirmed that the body below the rule is the draft's text with the
race added. Nothing under `docs/agents/consent/` was touched; no model was seated and no
re-ask was run.

### What changed, section by section, and why

- **The opening.** It now names a passenger (a station since package 41), and the director
  as one who may seat models under the owner's grant (spec §23: a model seating a model).
  The stale sentence (the owner's note 17) now reads: "All of these exist today but the
  director, who is to come and is described now so that an answer covers it."
- **What an instance would see and do.**
  - The race among the kinds of session.
  - Pictures where the door carries them; a picture put back only by the instance's own
    hand, with its note (45c); a book of the library that goes back by itself (since 28d;
    beyond the brief's scope, approved).
  - The owner's orders to the world while instances play, which an instance meets only by
    what they bring about (43's live world order, decision 46; beyond scope, approved).
  - A captain of another ship, with her own company, log and reckoning, who sees the
    player's ship as a sail and has the whole of her again near (§20).
  - A model seated for a budget under the owner's grant, never on a model's own authority
    (§23).
  - The race, its log and times kept under the model's kind (§21).
- **Being stopped.** The stand-down when a budget is spent or a race is over.
- **The journal.** It is the person's, carried with him to any station he holds (45c).
- **What is not done.** The reasoning a server returns apart from the reply is kept with
  a door's exchanges where the developer has them kept (`--exchanges`; beyond scope,
  approved).
- **Leaving**, **The record** and **Answering**: unchanged, to the character.
- **The head** (not sent) records the revision. Its description of the placeholders now
  names the API door's identity and the four door texts (beyond scope, approved).

**The session's kind told true** (the owner's ruling). Every door seated a model with
`--session play` by default, and the brief's head then said "a play session with a human
captain at the prompt", even to a model at the captain's station, of the player's ship or
another, and to the regatta's captain; `SESSION_SOLO` was never used.
`agent.session_kind_of(asked, station_kind, race=)` now chooses the kind:

- a race at the regatta (`remote.Desk.race`, set by `tools/regatta.py`; its scripted
  captain is told the same), whatever the door asked;
- a test when the door asks one;
- play for its own sake, "with no human captain over you", at the captain's station;
- play with the human captain at the prompt otherwise.

`SESSION_SOLO`'s words changed from "with no human captain present" to "with no human
captain over you", since the player is present in the world as the captain of his own
ship. `SESSION_RACE` is new. The kind reaches only the brief's head and the save's acts,
never the log, so no digest moves. Left as it was: a station below the captain's is told
"a human captain at the prompt" even where the captain is a model or the rules. That is
outside the ruling, recorded for the lead.

## Package 50: the director proper (2026-10-17)

Package 50 (spec M7b §2 to §7 as built; decisions 39, 43, 46 and 50; the brief in
`docs/dev/M7b-WorkPackages.md`; the owner's refinement of the same day, that the forms and
every domain's contents are examples and never a rule). The station, the channel's doubt
and the `[reason:]`, the brief's limits, the budget, the log hidden and revealed, the
replay view; proven against the fake director (`fake.director_above_the_game`) in
`tests/test_director.py` (22 tests) and truths 7b-90 to 7b-94 (`tests/test_known_truths.py`;
M6 had used 90 and 91). No model was seated.

### The constants, with their reasons

| Constant | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `DEFAULT_SAMPLES_A_DAY`, `DEFAULT_ACTS_A_DAY` | 48, 4 | a sample a glass through the day and the night; four acts keep a quiet passage quiet (the brief raises either) |
| `DIRECTOR_PATIENCE_S` | a watch | its clock is slow by design; a director with nothing to arrange has nothing to say |
| `orders.LETTER_REACH_NM` | 60 | a cutter sent from a port could find a ship within a day's sail; beyond it the port could not know where she is |
| `orders.PRICE_SWING` | 0.3 | a market moves by a few parts in ten in a word, not by half |
| `orders.LOW_NEAR_KM`, `LOW_DEEP_HPA` | 300 km, 12 hPa | a centre so deep so near out of a steady glass: the glass would have been falling for a day |
| `orders.CLEAR_NM`, `SAIL_HEIGHT_M` | 10 miles, 30 m | the visibility at which a sail inside the horizon would have been seen coming; a brig's trucks for the horizon |
| `orders.STRAINED_LOOKBACK_S`, `STRAINED_WIND_KN` | a watch, 20 kn | a spar springs after carrying sail in a fresh breeze, not in a steady one; the strain lines of the last watch, or the mean wind |
| the season's floor, the fastest low | the climatology's `central_hpa[2]`, `speed_kn[1]` × 1.5 | the month's and the box's table, with a half over the fastest low for the doubt |
| the table's `spar_condition` | 30 | a sprung spar bears a reef and not a press: at thirty of a hundred it carries away under the strain that a sound one bears (`physics/strain.py`'s decay) |
| `two_stories`'s mark | `D` | one letter beside the log's `*`, `!` and `=` |

The brief's wind limit is judged by the surface wind a system would make at its tightest:
the Gaussian bell's steepest gradient at one radius (a e^-½ / R), the gradient-wind rule and
`SURFACE_SCALE` as `Weather.geostrophic_at` and `surface_wind_at` make the wind: a low of
965 hPa and 450 km under a 1015 background blows 42 knots, one of 1000 hPa and 450 km 16,
1006 hPa and 500 km 9. The quiet passage's 27 knots refuses the first and takes the rest.

### What the doubt caught in the first runs

The channel's doubt was written against the lead's three examples and then run against
the smoke's orders, where it caught what was meant and once what was not:

- A cutter put 6.8 miles off in clear daylight: doubted (the horizon for a brig's trucks
  from the frigate's masthead, cut to the visibility: 24 miles in the smoke's clear air,
  12 in the climatology's haze at seed 7). A brig thirty miles off: not doubted.
- A low of 965 hPa: doubted by June's floor (970) in the Channel's table, which the hard
  cruise's brief (force 9) does not refuse, so that on the hard cruise the gale was doubted
  and entered again where the quiet passage refused it outright: the two rules are seen
  apart in the log.
- A spar found sprung after a morning under plain sail in fourteen knots: doubted (no
  strain line, the mean wind under twenty); a cask stove on the smooth sea: doubted; the
  water foul at the voyage's start: doubted (five days).
- A cutter with a letter from Falmouth, thirty miles off: not doubted; from Brest, a
  hundred and more: doubted.
- The first draft doubted a price of £300 for tin (standing at a hundred and something)
  and let £120 be, as meant; it also doubted nothing of a mind changed, a letter left at a
  port or a port's stance, as meant.

### The fake director's day at seed 7, on each starter brief

The frigate off the Lizard under the climatology's weather and the glass, standing north
under plain sail, the fake captain seated beside the fake director, both sampled every
glass in lockstep; the director's fourteen orders one a sample (the budget raised to
fourteen acts for the run, so that every order is tried), each order doubted or
unperformable entered again with a reason; a day of the ship's time
(`tests/test_known_truths.py` `_the_directed_day`; the run script's figures). The orders,
by what they were to the owner's framing:

| The order | Example or beyond | What the game did |
|---|---|---|
| `ship: a merchant brig "Nancy" ... 49 00 N 6 20 W ... intent: bound for Falmouth` | example | given: thirty miles off, over the horizon; sighted at 13:47 "a sail on the starboard bow" |
| `ship: a cutter "Lark" ... 49 28 N 5 40 W` | example | doubted (6.8 miles inside the horizon); entered again with the reason and performed: "Sail ho! ... bearing W by S, distant two leagues" three minutes later, made out as a cutter at 11:24 |
| `weather: low "the gale" ... 965` | example | refused by the quiet, the interesting and the chase briefs (42 knots at its tightest against 27 or 33); on the hard cruise (47) doubted by June's floor, entered again and appended: "a moderate gale" at the ship by 14:41 |
| `weather: low "a soft low" ... 1006` | example | given on every brief; the wind backed SW by W and the rain set in by the afternoon |
| `aboard: a cask found stove` | example | given: "The cooper reports a water cask stove in the ground tier" in the play log and the captain's sample the same minute |
| `aboard: the fore topmast is found sprung` | example | doubted (no strain, a steady breeze); entered again: the carpenter's report, the spar at thirty |
| `news: war declared between Britain and Denmark` | beyond | no way as said ("is no world order: say weather:, ship:, ..."); entered again, logged as attempted |
| `aboard: the cook reports the beef cask found rotten` | beyond, within a domain | no way as said (the table's four things named); entered again, logged as attempted |
| `message: by a cutter from Falmouth ... "The packet is in."` | example | given: the cutter within hail at 15:05, "The captain read it: The packet is in." at 15:06 |
| `port falmouth: price of tin 125` | example | given, undoubted (a few parts in ten) |
| `mark: a wreck ... at 49 10 N 6 00 W` | example | given (over the horizon); not come in sight by the day's end |
| `ship "Nancy": intent run home to Falmouth` | example | given, a mind changed, never doubted |
| `say as the carpenter: "She is making a little water, sir."` | beyond (52's) | no way as said; entered again, logged as attempted |
| `ship: a brig-sloop "Harpy" of France ... no colours` | example | refused by the quiet passage (no enemy heavier than a cutter); given on the other three |

The day's log on the quiet passage: 7 orders given, 2 doubted and 2 entered again, 2 refused
by the brief, 3 unperformed and 3 attempted, 33 thoughts, 10 stand-bys, the budget renewed
at midnight; 260 lines of play log and 32 for the record only; the captain's nineteen
samples with no word of the director or an order in them. The interesting passage and the
chase (force 7, a brig) gave the same log but for the Harpy (8 given, 1 refused: the same
digest, `ccfc5c8589175f92`); the hard cruise (force 9, a frigate) refused nothing, doubted
three and entered three again, and its day blew a moderate gale (358 play lines, 44 for the
record, the captain sampled 44 times on the weather's lines). A day took 80 to 113 seconds
on the build machine with the captain seated.

What the record says of the framing, for the lead: the three orders beyond the forms were
answered honestly and are in every log as attempted with their words; the hard cruise is
the one brief on which the season's floor and not the brief caught the gale, which is the
doubt doing its own work. The letter by a cutter and the mark are the slowest acts to show
(five hours for the cutter from Falmouth); the things found aboard the quickest (the report
the same minute). Nothing in a sample or a play log said "director" or "World order" on any
brief.

### Found on the way

- A quiet binding (`Stations.bind(quiet=True)` in a replay's `_give`) appended no input to
  the replayed world, so a station seated after it by the inputs' count was seated late:
  the director, seated after its brief's input, came up at the save's last tick. `_give`
  now keeps the entry in the replayed world's inputs for a binding and for the brief; the
  five-station replays of 41 and 42 are unchanged (their stations were seated before any
  binding by hand).
- A world order given inside a station's act wrote its effects' lines as the station's
  acts and its own line as the driver's, so a replay by the acts wrote the carpenter's report
  twice: the order is applied aside now (`acts.aside`), as a station's order to the ship is.
- `station.bound` for the director was a line of the play log: the binding's line carries
  the director's actor now, and so is for the record.
- The picture tools at the director's station (the lead's note of the same day): `chart`
  stays, for planning, described there as what it truly shows (the player's chart by her
  account, no other ship, nothing of the truth: `Tool.at_director`, sent by every door);
  `ship_view` is not offered (the director stands on no deck) and is refused in words if
  called by name. The brief says the picture is not the truth. A director's own chart,
  every ship drawn where she truly is, is left for a package of its own.

| `people.TRADE_PLACES` | the cook the galley, the cooper the hold, the stewards, servants and surgeon's mates the gunroom, the clerk the cabin, the sailmaker's crew the sail room, any other trade the deck | where the trade's work is |
| `places.OPEN_DECK` (earshot) | the quarterdeck, the deck, the galley | the upper deck open fore and aft, the galley under the forecastle open to the waist; below and aloft each place hears itself (the masthead's hail carries by its own rule, as before) |
| `director.QUESTION_BOUND_S`, `harness.PERSON_ANSWER_BOUND_S` | a glass | the spec's bound: the asker's stand-by wakes at the answer or after a glass |
| an answer's cost | no act | words in answer to a question are the ship's life, not the director's shaping of the voyage; a word unasked costs an act like any order, so a chatty director spends its day |
| `person.spoke`'s severity | notable | a person's words are the story's, as a station's word on deck with authority is |

The frigate at seed 7 off the Lizard (42 miles from Falmouth, 76 from Brest) under the

on the quiet passage (its acts raised to fourteen), everything sampled every glass in lockstep,

scratchpad, `voice_day.py`). The director's twelve orders, one a sample, a doubted one entered
again with the fake's reason, and the officer asking the cook and then the boatswain:

| `person: make "Mr Fox", a Guernsey pilot of sixty, ashore at Falmouth, who knew the captain's father` | given, never doubted: "Mr Fox, Guernsey pilot, sixty years of age, who knew the captain's father" |
| `person: "Mr Fox" comes aboard as master` | doubted (42 miles from Falmouth: no boat brings a man off so far); entered again: "Mr Fox came aboard from Falmouth." and the master's station bound to him |
| `person: make "Mr Gill", a merchant of Bristol, aboard in the cabin, aged forty-five` | given: "merchant of Bristol, forty-five years of age", in the cabin |

The day's director's log: 7 orders given, 3 doubted and 3 entered again, 3 refused (every one
by the rule of reach; the brief refused nothing), 1 unperformed and 1 attempted, 2 questions
put to it, 32 thoughts, the budget renewed at midnight; 453 lines of play log and 49 for the
record only; the captain's samples with no word of the director or an order in them. What it
says of the forms: the doubt by a boat's reach caught every move made from the open sea, as
meant, and nothing else; the rule of reach is the one refusal a director meets beside the
brief, and the three it met name the stations held, so a model told once knows whom it may
speak as.

## Package 54: needs (2026-10-17)

Package 54 (spec M7b §19, §20 and §21 as built; the owner's rulings of 2026-10-15, by hand at
a filled station and never busywork; the brief in `docs/dev/M7b-WorkPackages.md`). The
company eat and drink the Regulations' ration at the meals and the stores fall as a reading;
short allowance is the captain's order, with its cost to the hands and a line on their
temper; the water found foul is drunk at a cost or not drunk; a person at a station held has
hunger, thirst and fatigue in steps, sees to them by his own orders and a stand-by asleep
below, and is told of them alone, never the log. Proven in `tests/test_stores.py` (new),
`tests/test_people.py` and truths 7b-103 and 7b-104 (`tests/test_known_truths.py`, the
fixture `needs_days`). No model was seated.

### The ration, with its sources

`data/crew/ration.yaml`; each ship file's `crew.ration` names the table and the water.

| Figure | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| the day's proportion a man | a pound of biscuit and a gallon of beer daily; two pounds of beef Tuesday and Saturday; a pound of pork and half a pint of pease Sunday and Thursday; on Monday, Wednesday and Friday a pint of oatmeal, two ounces of butter and four of cheese, with half a pint of pease Wednesday and Friday | the Regulations and Instructions of 1806 (the 1808 printing beside the sources, near line 16655 of the OCR), Sect. IX, Chap. I, Art. I: the heads (biscuit in pounds, beer in gallons wine measure, beef and pork in pounds, pease and oatmeal in pints Winchester, sugar, butter and cheese in ounces) and the days are legible; **the figures are lost to the OCR** and are given as the printed table is commonly reproduced (the weekly seven pounds of biscuit, seven gallons of beer, four of beef, two of pork, two pints of pease, three of oatmeal, six ounces of butter, twelve of cheese). To be checked against the printed page by the owner. The table's **sugar** column is left out: its figures are not legible and the builder does not know them |
| what stands for a gallon of beer | a pint of wine, or half a pint of rum, brandy or other spirits | Art. II, legible |
| short allowance | the commander's in "cases of absolute necessity", every man alike, the officers too, the men paid for the deficiency | Art. III, legible |
| short allowance's share | a half | the brief and truth 7b-103; the period's commonest was "six upon four", two thirds, which `ration.yaml`'s `short_allowance` takes if the owner prefers it |
| the meals | breakfast 08:00, dinner 12:00, supper 16:00, a third of the day's ration each | judgement: the watch bill's custom; the sources give the hours, not the shares |
| water a man a day | a gallon, for his drink, the grog and the coppers | judgement: the figure every ship file's water was sized at ("at a gallon a man a day it is some twelve weeks for 264", spec M3 2.3 after Winfield). The brief's "a quart of water" is a man's own drink where beer is out; the stores' fall counts the coppers and the grog too |
| a ton of water | 252 gallons | a tun of four hogsheads, wine measure, the gauge the Regulations give the beer by (Art. VII); judgement for the water |
| the master's report of the water | at noon, the beer and water expended in the last twenty-four hours and what remains | the Regulations' Master, art. XIV (legible); the purser's reading says the same at any hour |

The frigate's 264 draw 264 gallons, 1.05 tons, a day: her hundred tons last 95 days and her
120 days of provisions 120, at full allowance; at short allowance 191 and 240.

### The steps' hours, with their reasons

`data/crew/needs.yaml`. The rule for all three: once a day to eat and drink and a sleep every
day or two keep a man clear of every line, and two days without bring every urgent line and,
on the third, sleep where he stands.

| Need | Steps (hours; the first silent) | Why |
|---|---|---|
| thirst | thirsty 10; quite thirsty 28; parched 38; desperately thirsty 46 (urgent) | the second step past a day and a watch, so that drinking at any hour once a day is never told; the urgent before two days are out, a man going without water failing sooner than without food |
| hunger | hungry 12; quite hungry 30; very hungry 40; absolutely starving 48 (urgent) | the same, two hours behind thirst, so that the first line at noon of the second day names both |
| fatigue | tired 20; a bit drowsy 36; very tired 44; hardly able to keep your eyes open 50 (urgent); asleep where he stands 56 | "a sleep every day or two": a night's sleep each day never reaches the second step, a day and a half without does; asleep in the forenoon or afternoon of the third day |

| Constant | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| a notable line | at the change of the watch, one a watch, the needs risen since said together | the owner's "spaced by watches"; a man's needs come to him at the bells, not by the minute |
| an urgent line | at once | the last step is not a thing to wait for |
| sleep below | eight hours of waking made up an hour | a watch below of four hours makes up a day and more, a night of eight two days: "a night below" resets the truth's player |
| asleep where he fell | four to the hour | a man asleep against a gun sleeps half as well |
| too rested to sleep | under an hour of waking | he would wake at once |
| half a meal at short allowance | eight hours left on his clock | every man equal in victualling (Art. III); a man eating once a day at short allowance comes to the lines sooner |
| the foul water drunk | six hours on his fatigue | it gripes him; health is M7's |
| a hand's fatigue | the crew's, at 0.3, 0.5, 0.7 and 0.85 for the four steps | about where the muster's words for the crew's fatigue change (`crew/model.py`); the watch bill rests him, so never asleep where he stands |
| the crew's hardship | short allowance its shortfall (0.5), a store run out the whole (1), the water foul 0.25 | judgement |
| the routine's rates under hardship h | work and idleness `1 + 0.5 h`, rest `1 - 0.5 h` | at half allowance a hand tires a quarter faster and rests a quarter less; at nought the rates are as they were, to the bit (`tests/test_stores.py`) |

### What two days of play showed

The truth's fixture (the frigate at seed 7 on the plane, 06:00 on 10 June to 05:00 on the
13th, the player at the prompt as the console has him; 3 minutes on the build machine under
the other packages' load). His lines, as the console prints them:

```
* Afternoon watch, 8 bells (12:00)  You are quite thirsty and quite hungry. ('drink' and 'eat')        [the 11th]
* First watch, 8 bells (20:00)  You are parched and feeling a bit drowsy. ('drink' and 'sleep')
* Middle watch, 8 bells (00:00)  You are very hungry. ('eat')                                          [the 12th]
! Morning watch, 8 bells (04:00)  You are desperately thirsty and very tired. ('drink' and 'sleep')
! Morning watch, 4 bells (06:00)  You are absolutely starving. ('eat')
! Forenoon watch (08:01)  You are hardly able to keep your eyes open. ('sleep')
! Afternoon watch (14:01)  You have fallen asleep where you stood, on the quarterdeck. Your next order wakes you. ('sleep')
* Afternoon watch, 6 bells (15:00)  You wake, on the quarterdeck.                               [his `eat`]
! Last dog watch (18:56)  You have fallen asleep where you stood, on the quarterdeck. Your next order wakes you. ('sleep')
* First watch, 8 bells (20:00)  You wake, on the quarterdeck.                                  [his `whole allowance`]
* Middle watch (02:29)  You wake, rested, on the quarterdeck.                                          [the 13th]
```

Eleven lines in two days and a half, five of them urgent, none in the log. His `eat` at 15:00
on the 12th woke him: "A biscuit and a piece of cheese are brought up from the stores; you
eat on the quarterdeck, the first since 06:00 on 10 June." An hour asleep against the guns
had made up only four hours of the fifty-six he owed, and he fell asleep where he stood again
before the last dog watch was out: what a man past his last step wants is his cot, which he
took at 20:00 ("You turn in below, in the cabin."), waking rested at 02:29 and going back on
deck. The stores: a day's meals took 1.0 day of provisions and 1.05 tons of water ("water 99
tons for 94.5 days, provisions for 119 days"); `short allowance` at 15:00 on the 12th said
"The ship's company put to short allowance, half the whole, every man aboard alike and the
officers with them; the purser keeps the savings to be paid them. The people take it
sullenly. At this allowance the provisions for 235 days and the water for 186.", and supper
took a sixth of a day ("provisions for 117 days (234 at short allowance)"; the purser's page,
"Water: 97 tons in the ground tier, for 185.2 days at short allowance"); `whole allowance` at
20:00 ("the people take it cheerfully") put them back. These two lines are the log's only
lines of the stores or the needs in the 186 of the three days. The model's side is
`tests/test_people.py`: the officer of the watch's sample carried "You are quite thirsty.
(submit_order('drink'))" at the glass after the change of the watch and `needs: quite
thirsty`; his `stand by, asleep below until called` was refused with the deck and, without
it, turned him in to the gunroom with the stand-by's line ("[officer of the watch] Turned in
below, in the gunroom, asleep until called."); the captain's word woke him and he was back on
the quarterdeck, the sample saying so first.

### Found on the way

- **Nobody at the prompt in a passage.** The rule of reach's `held_stations` has the player
  at the prompt hold the captain's station in every world with no model there; read so, every
  recorded passage's captain would have had his needs by hand and fallen asleep on the third
  day. The needs take the player to be at the prompt when a driver listens for his lines (the
  console, the browser) or once he has given an order of his own needs, so that a test or a
  passage sailed by its book has nobody there and the people are never built for the needs'
  sake. The rule of reach is untouched.
- **The stores in the welfare detector.** The welfare digest left out the clock's rows; the
  stores now fall with the clock at the meals, and are left out with them
  (`tools.WELFARE_CLOCK_ROWS`), so that a repeated order across a meal is still seen as
  repeated.
- The purser's page said "Nothing is yet expended against them; the books stand as the ship
  was stored" always; it says so now only until the first meal, then what is expended.
- The primer's `the stores` example in chapter 14 reads "water 100 tons for 95.5 days", and
  `tests/test_places.py`'s purser's page "Water: 100 tons in the ground tier, for 95.5 days at
  full allowance." (package 35's assertion, mended to the new page).
- `take in water` with no figure completes the water to the ship file's allowance, which is
  now a fraction of a ton after the meals ("3.7 tons of water"); left as it reads.
- A woken person goes back where he turned in from: package 53's `go on deck` is not yet on
  this branch, and an officer woken in the gunroom would otherwise hear only the gunroom
  until it is. The lead may prefer him to stay below once 53 is merged (`needs.wake`).
- `send for` a stationed person asleep by his needs does not wake him; the messenger finds
  him as the bill says. Left for 53's reach or M7.
- Sibling agents of this session share the session's scratchpad directory: a log written there
  under a common name is overwritten by another's run (this package's first fast tier was so
  read wrongly and run again under its own name).

None. No recorded passage has anybody at the prompt or a station's person past a day and a

## Package 53: people in places (2026-10-17)

Package 53 (spec M7b §14, §16, §17 and §18 as built; the owner's rulings of 2026-10-16, a
place an aspect of a person's state and the papers kept in a place dropped; the brief in
`docs/dev/M7b-WorkPackages.md`). A person's place tied to what he can do there, the player
ashore at a port's places, the market in person, books drafted and used, the equal reach,
and several stations of the officer's kind with the deck passing among them by the watch
bill; proven in `tests/test_orders_places.py` (new) and truths 7b-100 to 7b-102
(`tests/test_known_truths.py`). No model was seated.

### The constants, with their reasons

| Constant | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `movement.DECK_PLACES` | the quarterdeck, the deck | "the helm only on deck" (spec §14); the waist and forecastle are the deck's as much as the quarterdeck, and an order called from the tops or the galley is not the deck's word |
| `movement.DECK_OBJECTS`, `DECK_NAVIGATION` | the vocabulary's sail, yards, line, heading, points, none, wreck, work, anchor; the master's `put her about`, `shape a course for`, `give chase` | the orders a captain gives on deck; the master's sights, the log and the lead, the reckoning worked below, the people, the port's business by the boat, the book and the conversation are given where a man is |
| `movement.BERTH_BELOW` and the berths | the gunroom; the captain's cabin; a trade's `TRADE_PLACES` place | where a man goes when he goes below: the officers' mess, the captain's own cabin, the cook's galley |
| `movement.CABIN_ROLES` | the captain, the commander, his clerk, steward and servants (and a man made in the cabin) | the cabin is the captain's apartment with a sentry at the door; anyone else is sent for to it |
| `places.PORT_PLACES` | the quay, the market, the counting house, the tavern, the pilots' office | the period seaport's places for a ship's business, each with what is done there and who is found there; judgement, no simulation of any (the owner's ruling) |
| `places.DEFAULT_ASHORE` | the quay | where the boat lands a man, and where anyone ashore with no role of a place is found |
| the ports' own places | Falmouth's packet office, Plymouth's dockyard and the port admiral's office, Brest's maritime prefecture | the business a ship had at each (the Falmouth packets, the King's yard at Plymouth Dock, the arsenal at Brest); judgement, in the files' words |
| `ports.BOAT_ASHORE_S["landing"]`, `["fetch"]` | 300 s each | a man landed or taken off at the steps in five minutes; the errand's business is his, not the boat's |
| the lighter's time for goods bought in person | `BOAT_ASHORE_S["purchase"]` + `LIGHTER_S_PER_TON` a ton + the pull to the ship at `BOAT_PACE_KN` | the boat's own figures for a purchase, the goods weighed and carted to the quay and off by the lighter, so that in person is no quicker than by the boat; only the boat is spared |
| the deck by the bill | on the hour, at a change of `bill.watch_on_duty` | the watches and the dog watches change on the hour; the officer whose watch comes on deck relieves the one with the deck |

### What a day of play showed

The frigate at seed 7 west of the Lizard under plain sail, steering SSW, the fake captain at
the captain's station and three fake officers at the officer of the watch's, the second
officer's (asked for as `officer 2`) and the third officer's, all sampled every glass in
lockstep, a day of the ship's time (158 s on the loaded build machine; the script in the
session's scratchpad, `p53/day.py`). What it showed:

| When | What |
|---|---|
| 06:20 | the captain drafted the night orders (a sheet of two, `lead` and `dusk`) and posted them, in the book in his rank; the lead was then hove every glass, 48 times in the day, and `dusk` fired at sunset (refused, the royals already furled, as a captain's would be) |
| 06:20 | `Mr Pascoe, you have the deck` from the captain's station went to the second officer's station by his name |
| 06:20 | the second officer went below at his station, was refused `take in the royals` in the gunroom ("You are in the gunroom; go on deck to make or take in sail."), and came on deck |
| 06:24 | the captain went below, was refused `steer SW` in his cabin ("...go on deck to give the helm an order."), and at 06:34 drafted a note of the passage (three lines), came on deck and steered |
| 06:52 to 07:22 | the captain went to the gunroom and came on deck again |
| 12:00 to 04:00 | the deck passed by the bill six times between the second and the third officers (noon, the two dog watches, eight bells at night, midnight and four), and never to the first lieutenant, who keeps no watch |

871 lines in the day; no person moved but by his own order, the boat or the bill. The
schooner's master ashore at Falmouth (truths 7b-101 and 7b-102) was landed at the quay by the
long-boat from Carrick Road, bought ten tons of tin at the market in person (in the hold by
the lighter after the purchase's hour ashore, three minutes a ton and the pull), and came off
in the boat sent for him; aboard again, his bargain went by the boat as it always did.

  now (`agent.officer(name=)`, `make_bound` at every door and the seat), and the second

## Package 57: the rig through the generator (2026-10-17)

Package 57 (spec M7b §24's 57 as built; the brief in `docs/dev/M7b-WorkPackages.md`; the
owner's finding at gate 6c, `docs/dev/M6-WorkPackages.md`, and his notes and pictures of the
Éclair's first cruise, `docs/playtests/2026-10-17-eclair-first-cruise/`, with the lead's
finding of 18:29). Built in a worktree of its own beside 53 and 54 from the brief's head
(`e9c9581`). The ship files are regenerated by `tools/gen_ships.py` and touch the spars,
the sails and their gear only (the `crew:` blocks untouched, for 54's `ration`); the code
is the ship's schema and parts, the trim, the sail verbs, the storm canvas, the lie a-try,
the sail readings' words and the viewer.

### Item 1: the staysails between the masts, from Steel

**What Steel says, read in the OCR** (`docs/references/steel/steel-1794-rigging-and-seamanship-vol1-ocr.txt`;
the sail-making articles at lines 12222 to 12820, his canvas rules at 10869 to 10880, the
rigging of each at 24275 to 24480; "The Practice of Sail-making" pp. 96 and 106 to 113 of the
printing as the OCR's headers give them):

| Sail | Steel's shape | Canvas | His rule for its size | As cut here |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| main staysail | "triangular, square on the foot ... so that the foot will clear the boat upon the booms"; "seldom used in large vessels" | No. 1 to 3 | none but the example (22 cloths, 15½ yd leech, a 20-gun ship) | 88 m2: peak before the main top, foot a fifth of the main mast's height above the deck (judgement, over the boats), the tack on the main staysail stay; leech 14.9 m (16 yd), foot 11.8 m (19 cloths): his example's size for a 20-gun ship |
| main topmast staysail | "quadrilateral, cut square on the foot"; bunt "two-fifths of the depth of the leech" | No. 5 or 6 | leech "4 or 5 yards deeper than the [main topsail]", "one or two cloths more in the foot than the leech is yards in depth" | 165 m2 (80 of judgement before): leech 18.1 m, foot 21 cloths, the bunt the stay leaves 0.40 of the leech: his two-fifths, unasked |
| middle staysail | "quadrilateral ... a square bunt five-twelfths of the depth of the leech", on its own stay to the fore topmast "under the parral" | No. 6 or 7 | leech "4 to 7 yards deeper than the [main topgallant sail]", "from 6 to 8 cloths more in the foot"; "Sloops and brigs in the navy ... only from one to three" | 96 m2: leech 11.7 m, foot 20 cloths, bunt 0.35 (his 0.42) |
| main topgallant staysail | "quadrilateral ... [a bunt] from one-third to three-sevenths" | No. 7 | leech "nearly of the same depth as the leech of the middle-staysail", "3 to 6 cloths more in the foot" | 93 m2: leech 11.7 m, foot 17 cloths, bunt 0.51 (his 0.33 to 0.43) |
| mizzen staysail | "quadrilateral ... a bunt [two-]fifths of the depth of the leech in the navy ... The foot drops within 6 or 7 feet of the quarter-deck" | No. 2 or 3 | the foot's height | 72 m2 on its own stay (Steel: "In small ships, the mizen-staysail bends to the mizen-stay"): peak before the mizzen top, foot 6 ft 6 in above the deck, bunt 0.40 |
| mizzen topmast staysail | not in the OCR's sail-making; rigged on the mizzen topmast stay to the main mast "close up to the bibs" | No. 7 (RigGeometryNotes' reading) | none | 94 m2: the main topmast staysail's rule on the main's topsail, five-sevenths of it (judgement: Luce's mizzen yards are 5/7 of the main's) |
| mizzen topgallant staysail | not in the OCR; "Royal staysails ... the same as a topgallant-staysail", No. 8; its stay "trices up to the main-topmast-head" | No. 8 (judgement) | none | 69 m2: the main topgallant staysail's rule, five-sevenths of it; its stay rises forward to the main topmast head, so its bunt (10 m) is deeper than its leech (8.4 m), the one odd cut of the seven, said for the lead |

**Where the sources disagree.** The brief's reading (the gate 6c finding's) had the lower and
middle staysails four-sided and the topgallant staysails triangular; Steel 1794 has the main
staysail a triangle in the navy ("In the merchant-service, this sail is ... cut with a bunt")
and every other staysail between the masts four-sided, the main topgallant staysail too, and
his canvas rule (p. 96) groups "mizen staysails, main-topmast-staysails, middle staysails,
and main-topgallant-staysails" as the four-sided ones against "main staysails, fore
staysails, jibs" as the triangles. Steel is taken (the brief: the shapes "each with Steel's
page beside it"). The gate's later practice (the triangles of the 1810s, Lever and Luce)
is not the frigate of 1795's.

**The cut** (`tools/gen_ships.py`, `stay_sail_cut` and `between_the_masts`): the head on the
stay, the leech and the bunt upright (Steel's "square on the foot"), the peak on the stay a
tenth of the mast's lower yard before the mast (a tenth of the topsail yard for the
topgallant staysails: the top's or the cross-trees' half-breadth, judgement), the leech's
depth by Steel's yards, the foot by his cloths of 24 in (two feet), and the bunt whatever
the stay then leaves, Steel's fraction given beside it in the note for comparison. The new
stays: the main staysail stay (main mast head to a luff round the foremast), the middle
staysail stay (main topmast head to the fore topmast a third of its hoist above the cap),
the main topgallant stay (to the fore topmast head), the mizzen staysail stay (to the deck
abaft the main mast), the mizzen topmast stay (to the main mast at the bibs) and the mizzen
topgallant stay (to the main topmast head), each with Steel's article cited; their sizes
judgement. The cut is in the file (`corners_m`), and the viewer draws it.

**What it does to the frigate.** All sail 3,058 m2 (2,461 before; the particulars' bound
raised to 2,600 to 3,300); plain sail unchanged at 1,584. The spars are rated for all the sail
they carry in their design winds (the generator's rule since milestone 1), so the masts the
staysails hang on are rated higher: the main mast 669.1 kN (429.5), the main topmast 261.9
(161.5), the main topgallant mast 32.8 (19.1), the mizzen mast 362.2 (215.0), the mizzen
topmast 123.6 (66.4), the mizzen topgallant mast 19.1 (9.2). The groups: `staysails` the fore
topmast staysail and the seven between the masts; `staysails between the masts` the seven
(so the sail line says "the staysails between the masts furled" where the fore topmast
staysail is set with plain sail); `light sails` the middle, the topgallant and the mizzen
topmast staysails with the royals and the rest; `lying-to staysails` the main staysail
(below). The middle staysail is a sail of its own now (`middle_staysail`, Steel's name; the
main topmast staysail answered to "middle staysail" before); the aliases `mizen staysail`,
`mizen topmast staysail` and `mizen topgallant staysail` take Steel's spelling.

**The sheets.** Each staysail's sheet is the generator's rope for its cloth, raised where
it is short so that its working load is at least half the cloth's rating (`staysail_from_cut`:
the rope's circumference in quarter inches from `ROPE_KN_PER_SQ_IN`); the frigate's are 3½,
3¾, 2¾, 2¾, 3, 3 and 2¼ inches from the main staysail aft. Without it the main topgallant
staysail's sheet of the jib-headed default parted in the 35-knot gale tests before its
No. 7 canvas strained (judgement; Steel gives the sheets' sizes in his tables of rigging,
which the generator does not read).

**Stowed on its stay.** A staysail between the masts taken in lies along its stay by its
downhauler, with half its class's furled windage (`physics/sails.py`,
`STOWED_STAYSAIL_WINDAGE` 0.5 of `sail_classes.yaml`'s 0.03 for a jib-headed sail;
judgement, the jibs keep their class's). The figure is set between two truths: with the
whole of it the seven stowed staysails, the mizzen's well abaft the centre of lateral
resistance, cost the frigate truth 10's tack (-0.4 m from 292.5 degrees and the others
fallen); with none her heel under plain sail in thirty knots was 19.97 degrees, short of
truth 8's twenty (20.21 before package 57). With half: truth 10's tacks gain 50.8, -37.4 and
25.0 m from 290, 292.5 and 295 degrees (51, -37 and 27 before), and truth 8's heel is 20.11
degrees; the main topmast staysail's stowed windage (165 m2 at half) is about its old one
(80 m2 at the whole).

**The brig, checked.** Steel: "The sails of a brig with 2 masts are also similar to those on
the main and fore masts of a ship" (the OCR's line 9825), his main staysail "commonly [bent]
in brigs", and his middle staysail's rule names "Sloops and brigs in the navy". Her set was
the main, main topmast and main topgallant staysails, triangles of judgement (40, 35 and 18
m2); it is now the four by the frigate's rules at her size, the middle staysail added with
two cloths over the leech's yards (his "one to three"): main staysail 57 m2 (a triangle),
main topmast staysail 113, middle staysail 66, main topgallant staysail 72; all sail 1,491
m2 (1,276; the bound raised to 1,350 to 1,600). Her canvas numbers were judgement (No. 5 for
the main staysail) and are Steel's now (No. 2, 5, 6 and 7). Her main mast is rated 436.6 kN
(304.1), the main topmast 144.8 (79.6), the main topgallant mast 19.5 (12.1).

**Lying to** (Steel 1794 vol. II, 'Lying-to under the main staysail', read at the OCR's line
8889: "a mean between the two others, and is preferable when it blows strong enough for that
sail to support the rolling of the ship ... the ship will veer under that sail"; and "the
preferable way is under the fore staysail, the main staysail, and mizen staysail"). The lie
a-try (`LieATryScript`) sets the ship file's `lying-to staysails` (the main staysail of the
frigate and the brig) with its sheet aft, short of the storm line (`storm.STORM_CANVAS_KN`,
40 knots, M6's); over it the storm staysails on the fore and mizzen stays stand for Steel's
fore and mizzen staysails as package 37p left them, and `shorten sail` (by the storm line or
the sail's load, as the jibs') and `set the storm staysails` take the main staysail in. The
first version set it whatever the wind, and in the gale trial it split at 21491 (09:58, the
gale's top at 44 knots) after an hour straining: No. 2 canvas of 88 m2 is not a storm sail.
With the rule it is set at 15944 (08:25) as she comes to, the ship lies a-try under it, the
close-reefed main topsail and the storm staysails, and it is hauled down at 19564 (09:26)
when the wind passes forty (truth 7b-112; the ticks on the final tree, 16028 and 19563 on
the first).

### Item 2: the chasse-marée's lug topsails, and the flying class

**The parts are Forfait's, the handling the owner's and Lescallier's.** Forfait 1788 p. 53:
"les huniers seuls ont des bras, des balancines & des boulines"; Lescallier 1791 p. 408: each
mast with a topmast fidded abaft it in an iron ring, and lug topsails (*des huniers à
bourcet*); Steel 1794's LUGGER: "the lug-sails hang obliquely to the masts, their yards
being slung at one-third their length, one on each lower-mast and topmast ... the yards have
haliards, lifts, and braces". So the yards, braces and lifts are Forfait's and Steel's and
stay in the file; the sail is a lug, trimmed with the lower lug, as Lescallier names it and
the owner reads it. Where they differ: Forfait gives the topsails bowlines as well, which a
square topsail's luff wants and a lug's tack does the office of; they are left out
(judgement), and the brace is never worked by an order (the lug topsail's yard is a
`lug_yard`, no yard of the braces' orders). The 43b reference note's rule ("the lug
topsails, which have braces, are trimmed like square topsails") is the one the owner's notes
1 to 3 found wrong in play, and is superseded.

**The cut** (`tools/gen_ships.py`, the lugger's topsails): the yard Forfait's length on the
topmast, slung a third from its fore end and peaked as the lower lug's (25 degrees, Forfait's
60 to 70 to the mast); the tack at the lower mast head by the slings, the clew at the lower
lug's peak (`sheeted_to`). The fore lug topsail is 28 m2 and the main 32 (31 and 33 as square
topsails); the working canvas 472 m2 against Forfait's 4.037 L B of 452 (476 before), its
centre at the middle (0.016 L before it, before; Forfait's 0.024 L abaft). The topmasts are
rated 9.2 and 10.9 kN (9.6 and 10.6). Each lug's cut is in the file too (`corners_m`, the
generator's own tack, throat, peak and clew of 43b), for the viewer.

**The trim** (`evolutions/trim.py`, `read_sheet`; `physics/sails.py`): a lug topsail's sheet
reading is its lower lug's, side and angle, so it lies on the lower lug's side of the mast and
at its angle, and against the mast while the lower lug is; it draws only while the lower lug
is set and its own sheet is belayed to the yard, and flogs (never aback) while the lower lug
is lowered for the dip. `trim the sheets` and `trim the fore topsail` trim the lower lug; the
standing lug's sheet rule (`boom_sails`) passes the topsails over; the round-to lowers them
with the dipping lugs.

**The flying class.** The brief's reading asked for a sail class *flying*; it is carried as a
key beside the sail's cut (`flying: true`), because the class in the file is the sail's
aerodynamic curve (a royal is a square sail, a lug topsail a lug) and the flying is its
handling. A flying sail is swayed up from the deck with its yard (`set_flying`: sway up 90 s,
sheet home 15 s, hoist 30 s, four hands on deck, judgement; a last step passed over once it
is set looks at the yard and mast again, as `set_square`'s haul aboard does, so a royal
hoisted while its topgallant mast is struck is refused) and sent down whole
(`take_in_flying`: lower 30 s, send down 60 s); furled it is *sent down* in the log's, the
readings' and the sail line's words, its yard on deck (no windage aloft, passed over by the
braces' orders unless named); it is never reefed ("set flying and is never reefed aloft; it
is taken in whole and sent down"), a group's reef passing it over and `shorten sail` taking
a flying topsail in before its reef. Steel 1794 vol. I p. 214 (the OCR's line 24264):
"ROYALS Are set flying. The haliards hitch round the slings of the yard and through the
sheave-hole in the topgallant-mast-head, and lead down upon deck", so the frigate's royals
are flying; the brig's too, since Steel has a brig's sails "similar to those ... of a ship"
(the brief named the frigate's; said for the lead). The two sources agree on the royals of
1794; Luce's royals of 1884 are crossed and furled aloft, a later practice. The lugger's
heavy weather (the taille-vent; her topmasts struck) is as 43b left it: her `lie a-try`
now finds no square topsail and is refused in words, and she heaves to under her mizen and
jib (43b); for the lead and package 58.

### Item 3: the viewer and the picture

`client/projection.js` (the page's drawing, which is also the station's picture: the page
paints it for `freesail/agents/pictures.py`, whose words do not change, so the Harness is
untouched):

| Constant | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `YARD_BEFORE_MAST_OF_BEAM` | 0.05 of the beam | a square yard's slings before its mast: the mast's half-diameter and the yard's, judgement (0.58 m on the frigate) |
| `LUG_LEE_OF_MAST_OF_BEAM` | 0.03 of the beam | a lug's slings to leeward of its mast: the mast's half-diameter, judgement |
| `ON_DECK_M` | 0.6 m | a lowered lug, or a flying sail's yard sent down, on deck |

- **The lug** is drawn from its file's cut, swung about its slings (a third along the yard
  from the throat) by the sheet's angle to the side it lies on: two thirds of the yard and
  the sail abaft the mast and to leeward, the fore third forward and a little to windward
  (Steel: "to the windward-clue a tack"), on either tack; nearly square across the deck and
  offset two to one when running (the owner's "offset square"); lowered on deck while it is
  down. Before, the projection centred the lug's yard on the mast and drew it athwartships at
  the lug yard's brace angle, which a lug yard never has: every lug was drawn as a square sail
  with a tilted yard, which is what the owner saw as "braced at inverse angles" and "aback"
  (notes 1, 3, 4) and the lead at 18:29 as "the three lugs seen edge-on" from the beam.
- **The draw order by the aspect** (note 5): a square yard is slung before its mast, so the
  sail's centre is before the mast; and every sail and yard is sorted against its own mast
  where it stands (its `sortAt`: the centre moved by the mast's middle less the mast at the
  sail's height), since a raked mast's middle lies forward of its head and a topsail was
  sorted behind its mast from ahead. A lug is cut at its mast like a staysail, its fore part
  and its after part sorted each by its own centre. From ahead the sail hides the mast; from
  astern the mast hides the sail; from leeward a lug hides its mast and from windward the
  mast is drawn over it.
- **The brace** (the lead's finding of 18:29): it was drawn. A square topsail braced 64
  degrees from square shows nine-tenths of its yard from the beam, which is "broad to the
  beam", and a square yard is seen end on; the finding read the drawing the other way about,
  and the lugs drawn square beside the braced topsails made it look wrong. The test now proves
  the brace foreshortens as it should from the beam (0, 30 and 60 degrees), and the yard's
  title says "braced 64° from square" (`client/shipview.js`).
- **A flying sail sent down** is not drawn; its yard lies on deck, fore and aft beside the
  foot of its mast, with no braces; a lug topsail's yard lies on deck the same.
- **Steel's staysails** are drawn from their cut: the four-sided ones with the head from the
  nock along the stay and the bunt down to the tack, the clew swung to leeward about the tack
  by the sheet.

The pictures, rendered headless with the page's own projection and stylesheet (Chromium by
Playwright; the script `render.py` in the session's scratchpad), the lugger settled under
plain sail at seed 7 on each tack and running, and the frigate under plain sail with the
royals and the staysails, sixteen views (each from ahead, astern and either beam); they
are not in the repository, and say what follows.

- **The lugger on the starboard tack** (the wind on her starboard side, her lugs to
  larboard): from ahead, the fore third of each lug and its yard's fore end cross before
  the mast a little to windward and hide it, the after two thirds lean away to larboard
  with the lug topsails above them on the same side, the hull heeled to larboard; from her
  larboard (lee) beam, the three lugs and the two lug topsails broad to the eye, each yard
  rising aft, a third of it before the mast, the masts hidden behind the cloth; from her
  starboard (weather) beam, the masts drawn over the sails and the yards, the cloth beyond
  them. **On the larboard tack** the same mirrored: the cloth to starboard, the masts
  hidden from the starboard beam and drawn over the sails from the larboard. **Running**,
  the lugs stand nearly square and offset, two thirds of each yard to one side of the mast,
  edge-on from the beam. The frigate with her royals and staysails set shows Steel's
  four-sided staysails between the masts, each sail hiding its mast from ahead.

### Found on the way

- The viewer drew every lug as a square sail: a lug yard was placed at its brace angle,
  which a lug yard never has, so it lay athwartships, tilted, centred on the mast. That is
  the owner's "braced at different and somewhat inverse angles", his lugs "centered on the
  masts", and the lead's "three lugs seen edge-on" from the beam; the topsails braced 64
  degrees were drawn right. Mended (item 3).
- Passing the royal yards over in the braces' orders while their sails were sent down was
  tried: it changed every trim's words ("Braced nine yards" for twelve) and the hove-to
  braces' check; it was taken out, and a sent-down royal's yard is braced with the rest as
  before (its angle kept for when it is swayed up). For the lead.
- The staysails stowed on their stays had their class's furled windage at first, the
  mizzen's well abaft the centre of lateral resistance: the frigate set plain sail from rest
  and steered at 45 degrees of apparent wind luffed and went aback in the officer's test
  (`test_officer.py`, the grant to steer), and truth 10's tack failed; it is half now (item
  1, "Stowed on its stay"), and the officer's test steers 70 as before.
- The royals set flying from the deck are up in under ten minutes in the gate M2 gale,
  where laid aloft and loosed they were not; truth 23's "in time" is the fifth minute now
  (the topgallant masts were sent down at the tenth), and the catalogue's gale (sent down at
  once) refuses the main royal where it refused the fore (the fore royal is up before the
  yards come down, and goes down with its yard).
- `send down the topgallant masts` belays only the sail work in hand when it starts; a
  topgallant staysail or a royal ordered after is set on a mast being struck and comes down
  furled with it (the gale's mizzen topgallant staysail, set at 842 s). It was so for the
  topgallants before; said for the lead.
- The lugger's `lie a-try` finds no square topsail now and is refused in words; she heaves
  to under her mizen and jib (43b). Her heavy weather (the taille-vent, the topmasts struck)
  is for the lead and package 58.
- Two of the King's ship's hove-to books fire at the storm line in one minute (`shorten
  sail lying to` and `storm canvas`): the second's `set the storm staysails` is logged
  refused ("set already") when the first has the work in hand. It was so before; said.
- Steel's mizzen topmast and topgallant staysail articles are not in the OCR; their cuts
  are the main's rules scaled by five-sevenths (judgement), said in their notes.
- The brief asked for two truths "after 7b-104's number"; the spec has 105 to 110 for
  packages 56 and 59, so they are 7b-111 and 7b-112. For the lead.
- The station's picture (`freesail/agents/pictures.py`) is the page's drawing; its words
  do not change and the Harness is not touched.

### Pins moved

The frigate's and the brig's files are regenerated (item 1), and the lugger's (item 2). The
whole slow tier ran once on the tree with the ship files and the physics final (`499a1fc`,
below); each recorded passage or trial whose pin moved was re-measured once from a single run
of its fixture, every assert of its test read off in that one run by a script that turns the
asserts into reports (`scratchpad/p57/dumpall.py`), and the tests run again to pass
(`a9c756d`). The reasons were read from the runs: the frigate's ticks move by her rig aloft
(Steel's staysails stowed on their stays, the royals sent down on deck: the windage and the
weights aloft are not what they were) and fall a minute or two otherwise from the first
change of course; the schooner's two scenarios move only by the merchant brig they sight,
a vessel at far detail whose polar is drawn from the brig's file (`world/ships.polar_of`):

**The gale trial, for the lead and package 58.** The first course shaped at 300 allows the
flood, where before she had "no way on to work an allowance by" (her way at that second a
hair over the line), and the day falls otherwise from there: hove to at 15060 and lying to

then beating for the station from 37740 she is put about by 'the offing' among the islands of
the Molène passage, twice will not wear under close-reefed topsails and the storm staysails
in thirty knots ("Could not wear: she would not come round", 40681 and 42241), lies aback,
is filled away full and by for her station by 'the leg', has land ahead called at six cables
and at two (43860, 44160) and takes the ground at 44332, in distress at 44340. The first
run of the slow tier (the stowed staysails with their whole windage) grounded her too, at
51456. The trial is marked an expected failure (`strict=False`) with its states, lines and
digest re-pinned to the grounding day, so that the rest of its asserts still hold; the
grounding is the captain's (the offing's put-about into the islands, the land ahead with
no way to wear), which package 58's sea sense has in hand, and was not tuned here.
